Question: A train, an hour after starting, meets with an accident which detains it a half hour, after which it proceeds at \(\dfrac34\) of its former rate and arrives \(3\dfrac12\) hours late. Had the accident happened \(90\) miles farther along the line, it would have arrived only \(3\) hours late. The length of the trip in miles was:
Solution:
Both accident scenarios include the same half-hour stop. Their arrival times differ because a 90-mile stretch is traveled at the original speed in the second scenario instead of at the reduced speed.

For a fixed distance, reducing the speed to \(3/4\) makes the travel time \(4/3\) of its original value. The extra time is therefore \(1/3\) of the original travel time. Moving the accident 90 miles farther along saves \(3\frac12-3=\frac12\) hour, so the original travel time for those 90 miles is
\[
\frac{1/2}{1/3}=\frac32\text{ hours}.
\]
The original speed is consequently
\[
90\div\frac32=60\text{ miles per hour}.
\]
In the actual trip, the slower running accounts for \(3\frac12-\frac12=3\) hours of lateness. Again, this extra time is \(1/3\) of the normal travel time for the distance remaining after the accident. That remaining distance would normally take \(3\div\frac13=9\) hours. Including the first hour, the whole trip would normally take \(10\) hours, so its length is
\[
60\cdot10=\boxed{600\text{ miles}}.
\]
As a check, the reduced speed is \(45\) mph. The actual trip takes \(1+\frac12+540/45=13\frac12\) hours. With the accident 90 miles later, it takes \(150/60+\frac12+450/45=13\) hours. These are exactly the stated delays relative to the normal 10-hour trip. The answer is \(\text{C}\).
